title: The Walled Garden to the Far Shore: Ruskin, the Stones, and the Wealth That Is Life
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: London, Hunter Street: the only child
stops.date_confidence: attested; the two lenses of this dossier give the house as 51.5246/-0.1219 and 51.5262/-0.1225, and the second is used here
stops.campa: At 54 Hunter Street, off Brunswick Square, a son is born to John James Ruskin, a sherry merchant who has paid off his own father's debts to the last shilling, and to Margaret, his cousin and his wife, who reads the Bible aloud with the boy from end to end and then begins it again. He is the only child and he is not shared. The house holds no other children, few toys, and a growing collection of watercolours on the walls. He is taught that looking is a duty. The father who cleared those debts to the shilling reads every proof sheet his son writes for the next forty-five years.
suggested_refs: The site of 54 Hunter Street, Brunswick Square, London, birthplace of Ruskin

stops.name: Herne Hill, the garden of seventy trees
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month and day not recorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: The family moves out to a villa at 28 Herne Hill, where the garden holds some seventy trees inside its wall. He is tutored at home, kept from toys, and given the run of the fruit on the condition that he asks before he picks. Here he learns to read the veins of a leaf and the mortar of a wall with the same attention, and here, between Oxford terms, he will draft the notebooks that grow into The Seven Lamps of Architecture. Summers go north to Perth, to his mother's people at Bowerswell, a house he will one day marry in.
suggested_refs: 28 Herne Hill, South London, and its walled garden, described at length in Praeterita

stops.name: Calais, the first crossing
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the month is the tour's usual season, not a recorded date
stops.campa: John James Ruskin sells sherry to the great houses of England and takes his family with him on the rounds; in 1825 the rounds cross the Channel. At Calais the boy sets foot on the Continent for the first time, on a tour through France and Belgium that fixes the shape of a lifetime: a hired carriage, a sketchbook, a mother with the Bible, a father with the accounts, and a road running south. He will make the crossing again almost every year that his health and his work allow, and the last of those journeys is more than fifty years off.
stops.quote: The material which Nature furnishes, in any given country, and the form which she suggests, will always render the building the most beautiful, because the most appropriate
stops.quote_source: John Ruskin, The Poetry of Architecture (1837-38), Part I, section 53, Project Gutenberg ebook 17774
suggested_refs: The Calais packet and the 1825 Ruskin family tour of France and Belgium

stops.name: Herne Hill, the first printed poem
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of publication; the place of writing is inferred from the family residence
stops.campa: At ten he is writing verse in imitation of Byron and Scott, and his father copies the best of it out fair. In August the Spiritual Times prints 'On Skiddaw and Derwent Water,' the first of his words to reach the public, five years before he is sent to Thomas Dale's evangelical school at Peckham and seven before Oxford. The boy who will spend his life telling England what it is looking at begins by telling it about a mountain in Cumberland seen from a carriage window. Seventy years later he will be buried within sight of that country.
suggested_refs: 'On Skiddaw and Derwent Water,' Spiritual Times, August 1829, Ruskin's first publication

stops.name: Strasbourg, under the single spire
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the tour; month reconstructed from the itinerary
stops.campa: The tour of 1833 goes up the Rhine and over the passes, and at Strasbourg the boy of fourteen stands under the one unfinished spire of the cathedral. A present that spring, Samuel Prout's Sketches Made in Flanders and Germany, has already told him what to look for; the stone teaches the rest. He draws. From this front, by his own later account, the turn toward architecture begins: not toward building, which he never practises, but toward reading buildings as evidence about the people who cut them and the faith they cut them for.
stops.quote: It is, or ought to be, a science of feeling more than of rule, a ministry to the mind, more than to the eye.
stops.quote_source: John Ruskin, The Poetry of Architecture (1837-38), on architecture, Project Gutenberg ebook 17774
suggested_refs: The west front and spire of Strasbourg Cathedral, drawn by Ruskin on the 1833 tour

stops.name: Schaffhausen, the falls and the chain of the Alps
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month reconstructed from the itinerary
stops.campa: Below Schaffhausen the Rhine goes over its ledge in white water, and that same evening, from the road, the family sees the whole chain of the Alps standing along the southern horizon. In Praeterita, written sixty years afterwards by a man whose mind is failing, he sets this evening down as the hour his life was given its direction. Mountains are never scenery to him after this. They are structure and weather before they are a view, and he goes back to draw them in every decade of his working life.
stops.quote: What is most musical, will always be found most melancholy; and no real beauty can be obtained without a touch of sadness.
stops.quote_source: John Ruskin, The Poetry of Architecture (1837-38), Project Gutenberg ebook 17774
suggested_refs: The Rheinfall at Schaffhausen and the southward view toward the Alps described in Praeterita

stops.name: Milan, the marble front
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month reconstructed from the itinerary
stops.campa: The carriage crosses into Italy and the family stands before the marble front of Milan cathedral, a forest of pinnacles that the boy counts rather than admires. The tour runs on to Genoa and its harbour and turns homeward through Turin, a city that means nothing to him yet. Twenty-five years from now a painting in a gallery in that town will take his mother's religion away from him in a single afternoon. He is fourteen, he draws what is in front of him, and the notebook fills faster than the road unrolls.
suggested_refs: Milan Cathedral, Genoa harbour, and Turin, the Italian legs of the 1833 Ruskin family tour

stops.name: Venice, the first sight from the water
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; month reconstructed from the tour's autumn season
stops.campa: He is sixteen when the boat turns and Venice stands up out of the water. He calls it afterwards that Paradise of cities. The stones are already going: the Austrians hold the town, the palaces are let as lodgings, the sea is at the footings, and the restorers are at work with scrapers. He does not yet know that he will come back with a ladder and a measuring rod, that he will draw the capitals of the Doge's Palace one by one, or that the book he makes of it will be read at Oxford by a young man named William Morris.
suggested_refs: The Piazza San Marco and the Bacino, Ruskin's first view of Venice in 1835

segments.name: Christ Church and the Defence of Turner

stops.name: Christ Church, Oxford: the gentleman-commoner
stops.date_confidence: matriculation at Michaelmas 1836 attested; residence at Christ Church taken up January 1837
stops.campa: He comes up from Thomas Dale's school at Peckham to Christ Church as a gentleman-commoner, entered by his father among the sons of noblemen. His mother takes lodgings in the High Street for the whole of his residence and he drinks tea with her every evening of it. He is seventeen, has published verse, and has seen the Alps and Venice. He has never lived a day out of his parents' reach, and he does not begin now. The other gentlemen-commoners hunt and dine; he goes down the High Street to his mother.
suggested_refs: Christ Church, Oxford, and the High Street lodgings taken by Margaret Ruskin for her son's residence

stops.name: London, The Poetry of Architecture under a Greek name
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of first serialisation; month reconstructed
stops.campa: Under the name Kata Phusin, according to nature, an undergraduate publishes a series on the cottages and villas of Europe, arguing that a building is answerable to the ground it stands on and to the people who live in it. He is eighteen. The positions he will hold for sixty years are already in it: a nation's character legible in its stone, ugliness treated as a moral condition rather than a matter of taste. The essays are widely read and nobody knows who wrote them.
stops.quote: No man can be an architect, who is not a metaphysician.
stops.quote_source: John Ruskin, The Poetry of Architecture (1837-38), Project Gutenberg ebook 17774
suggested_refs: The Poetry of Architecture, serialised in Loudon's Architectural Magazine under the pen name Kata Phusin
sources: John Ruskin, The Poetry of Architecture, Project Gutenberg ebook 17774

stops.name: Oxford, the Newdigate Prize and the old poet
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year; the June date follows the ordinary Encaenia season
stops.campa: At the third attempt he wins the Newdigate Prize for poetry and recites the piece in the theatre. Wordsworth, in Oxford to be given an honorary degree, is present, and the two are introduced. The old poet who taught England to look at mountains meets the young man who will spend his life proving that looking at them accurately is a form of honesty. Ruskin is twenty. His health is already breaking under the work and the schools, and the degree he came for will have to wait another three years.
suggested_refs: The Newdigate Prize recitation in the Sheldonian Theatre, Oxford, 1839

stops.name: Fontainebleau, the aspen at the roadside
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction: the episode is told in Praeterita without a fixed date, and the month here is inferred from the tour
stops.campa: Oxford has just given him an unusual honorary double fourth, a degree shaped around a candidate whose illness broke his schools. He walks in the forest at Fontainebleau, low and without occupation, and lies down on the bank of the road before a spray of ivy and a young aspen. He draws it, line by line, as it actually grows rather than as drawing masters say a tree grows. By the account he gives in Praeterita the despair lifts as the drawing proceeds, and the principle of his whole criticism is settled on that bank.
suggested_refs: The forest road at Fontainebleau and the aspen study of 1842, told in Praeterita

stops.name: Denmark Hill, Modern Painters and the defence of Turner
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of publication; month reconstructed
stops.campa: The family moves to a larger house at 163 Denmark Hill, and out of its study comes an anonymous book signed only by a Graduate of Oxford. Modern Painters defends J. M. W. Turner, then old and mocked, against critics who preferred the brown varnish of the old masters, on the ground that Turner is simply the more truthful about cloud, stone, and water. To prove it the author has counted strata at Chamonix and watched the same peak in every weather. He is twenty-four. Four more volumes follow across seventeen years.
suggested_refs: 163 Denmark Hill, London, and the first volume of Modern Painters, 1843

stops.name: Lucca, the tomb of Ilaria del Carretto
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of the tour; month reconstructed from the itinerary
stops.campa: On his first Continental journey without his parents, twenty-six years old and travelling with a valet and a drawing master, he stops in Lucca before Jacopo della Quercia's effigy of Ilaria del Carretto in San Martino. He draws the folded hands and the small dog at her feet, and takes the tomb afterwards as his standard of repose in sculpture. The same tour gives him the Campo Santo at Pisa and the walls of Santa Maria Novella in Florence: the early Italians, working before Raphael, still telling the truth about what they saw.
suggested_refs: The effigy tomb of Ilaria del Carretto, San Martino, Lucca, drawn by Ruskin in 1845

stops.name: Bowerswell, the marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pin is the atlas's canonical Bowerswell coordinate carried from john_everett_millais.journey.json, which differs from this dossier's geographical correction of 56.396/-3.416
stops.campa: He marries Euphemia Chalmers Gray at Bowerswell in Perth, in the house where his mother grew up; neither of his parents attends. She is nineteen, quick, and made for company; he is twenty-nine and has just seen the second volume of Modern Painters through the press. The wedding journey goes to the Gothic churches of Normandy and Picardy, and the bridegroom spends it measuring the flamboyant tracery of Saint-Wulfram at Abbeville. The marriage is never consummated. It will end in a court six years from this morning.
suggested_refs: Bowerswell House, Kinnoull, Perth, where Effie Gray married Ruskin in 1848 and Millais in 1855

stops.name: Park Street, The Seven Lamps of Architecture
stops.date_confidence: publication attested to 1849; month reconstructed, and the Park Street residence is itself a reconstruction from secondary summaries
stops.campa: The couple keep house at 31 Park Street in Mayfair, near enough to the fashionable world for her and near enough to his books for him. From here he publishes The Seven Lamps of Architecture: seven conditions laid on building, sacrifice, truth, power, beauty, life, memory, and obedience, each of them moral before it is aesthetic. It is a book that treats a mason's dishonesty as a sin and the restoration of an old church as a lie told about the dead. Within thirty years it is the founding document of the campaign to leave old buildings alone.
stops.quote: When we build, let us think that we build for ever.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to John Ruskin, The Seven Lamps of Architecture (1849), 'The Lamp of Memory'; the primary text could not be reached to confirm the wording
suggested_refs: The Seven Lamps of Architecture, 1849, with Ruskin's own plates etched from his drawings
sources: WebFetch summary, Effie Gray marriage and residences

stops.name: Venice, the Hotel Danieli
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1849; day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: He brings Effie to Venice in November and takes rooms at the Danieli on the Riva, a step from the Doge's Palace. She dances at the Austrian officers' balls and is admired; he is out at seven in the morning in the wet cold with a ladder, a measuring rod, and a daguerreotype apparatus, taking down cornices before they fall. Two winters here fill notebook after notebook with plans, mouldings, and dates. Fifty-one years later, four months after his death, Marcel Proust takes a room in this same hotel to translate him.
suggested_refs: The Hotel Danieli on the Riva degli Schiavoni, Ruskin's base for the Stones of Venice campaigns and later Proust's
sources: WebFetch summary, Effie Gray honeymoon and Venice research

stops.name: Venice, the capitals of the Doge's Palace
stops.date_confidence: attested to the 1849-50 research campaign; month reconstructed
stops.campa: He works the arcade of the Doge's Palace capital by capital, drawing the carved foliage and the heads and dating each of them by the cut of the leaf. Nobody has done this before. He measures the Ca' d'Oro on the Grand Canal while a restorer is scraping the Gothic tracery off its front, and writes that he is taking the record of a corpse. The argument taking shape under the measurements is that the ornament of a building is the record of the workman's mind, and that a state's honesty can be read in its stone.
suggested_refs: Ruskin's measured drawings of the Doge's Palace capitals and the Ca' d'Oro, 1849-50

stops.name: London, the letters to The Times
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1851; day not recorded, defaulted to 01. Pin inherited byte-identical from john_everett_millais.journey.json
stops.campa: He is thirty-two and he does not know them. When the reviewers fall on the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood for painting with hard edges, bright ground, and no varnish, he writes twice to The Times in their defence, unasked, and adds a note on them to the next edition of Modern Painters. John Everett Millais and William Holman Hunt find themselves protected by the most feared critic in England. The friendship comes after the defence, not before it. Two years from now he will take Millais to Scotland to paint his portrait, and take his wife along.
suggested_refs: Ruskin's 1851 letters to The Times defending the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood

stops.name: London, The Stones of Venice
stops.date_confidence: volume I published 1851, volumes II and III 1853; the stop is pinned at the opening of the span and the month is reconstructed
stops.campa: The three volumes come out over two years, dated from the fall of a republic that once let its craftsmen think. In the chapter called 'The Nature of Gothic' he argues that the roughness of medieval carving is the mark of free men and that the finish of modern work is the mark of slaves. At Oxford, William Morris reads that chapter with Edward Burne-Jones and calls it a revelation; in 1892 he prints it by itself at the Kelmscott Press. He also campaigns for the rest of his life against the scraping of Saint Mark's.
stops.quote: You must either make a tool of the creature, or a man of him. You cannot make both.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to John Ruskin, The Stones of Venice, volume II, chapter VI, 'The Nature of Gothic'; the primary chapter could not be reached to confirm the wording
suggested_refs: The Kelmscott Press edition of 'The Nature of Gothic,' printed by William Morris in 1892 with his own preface

stops.name: Glen Finglas, the portrait against the gneiss
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1853; day not recorded. Pin inherited byte-identical from john_everett_millais.journey.json, which differs from this dossier's geographical correction of 56.230/-4.362
stops.campa: He takes Millais and Effie to the Trossachs for the summer so that Millais can paint him standing on the gneiss beside the falls of Glen Finglas. The party lodges at Brig o' Turk in a schoolmaster's cottage through rain that does not stop for weeks. Ruskin stands for the rock; Millais paints the rock with the geological exactness Ruskin himself taught the Brotherhood to want, and falls in love with Ruskin's wife while he does it. The portrait is finished the year after. The marriage does not last as long as the picture takes.
suggested_refs: Millais, 'John Ruskin at Glenfinlas,' begun 1853, finished 1854, Ashmolean Museum

stops.name: Edinburgh, the lectures on architecture and painting
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1853; day not recorded, defaulted to 01. Pin inherited from john_everett_millais.journey.json
stops.campa: In November he lectures in Edinburgh on architecture and painting to rooms that will not hold the audience, telling them that the war of the Pre-Raphaelites is still in front of them and that Scotland builds in a borrowed Greek suiting neither its weather nor its faith. He is at the height of his public authority and speaks without a note of trouble in his voice. Effie has gone back to Bowerswell; the letters passing between Perth and London are already about lawyers. Nobody in the hall knows it.
stops.quote: All unity of feeling (which is the first principle of good taste) is neglected; we see nothing but incongruous combination
stops.quote_source: John Ruskin, The Poetry of Architecture (1837-38), section 8, Project Gutenberg ebook 17774
suggested_refs: Ruskin, Lectures on Architecture and Painting, delivered at Edinburgh, November 1853
sources: John Ruskin, Lectures on Architecture and Painting (Edinburgh, 1853)

stops.name: London, the annulment
stops.date_confidence: suit filed April 1854 and decree granted July 1854, both attested; the day within July is not recorded
stops.campa: Effie leaves him in April, returns her wedding ring to his mother, and files for annulment on the ground that the marriage was never consummated. She is examined and found a virgin after six years of it. The decree is granted in July. Ruskin makes no defence, publishes not one word, and is taken abroad by his parents. The next year she marries John Everett Millais, who painted her husband standing on a rock in Scotland, and bears him eight children. Ruskin never marries again and never explains himself in print.
suggested_refs: The 1854 annulment suit of Gray v. Ruskin and its medical depositions

stops.name: Red Lion Square, the Working Men's College
stops.date_confidence: teaching attested 1854-1858; the month is reconstructed, and the pin is the college's first home in Red Lion Square, not the Great Ormond Street building it moved to in 1857
stops.campa: F. D. Maurice opens a college for working men in Red Lion Square and Ruskin takes the drawing class without pay, teaching clerks and joiners for four years. Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Ford Madox Brown, Edward Burne-Jones, and others teach beside him. He does not teach them to make pictures. He teaches them to see, on the principle that a man who can draw a leaf as it actually grows is harder to lie to afterwards. In 1857 the class moves with the college to Great Ormond Street.
stops.quote: Then FINE ART is that in which the hand, the head, and the _heart_ of man go together.
stops.quote_source: John Ruskin, The Two Paths (1859), Lecture II, 'The Unity of Art,' delivered at Manchester, 14 March 1859; Project Gutenberg ebook 7291
suggested_refs: The Working Men's College at 31 Red Lion Square, London, opened 1854

segments.name: Rose, Turin, and the Wealth That Is Life

stops.name: Denmark Hill, Rose La Touche
stops.date_confidence: the date is attested from Ruskin's own words; the place of the first meeting is not fixed by the sources and the pin is his residence
stops.campa: An introduction brings the La Touche family of County Kildare to him for drawing lessons. Rose is nine on the third of January, in his own phrase now rising towards ten; he is a month short of thirty-nine. He teaches her to draw, and she teaches him, he says afterwards, everything else there is. He will propose when she is eighteen, be told to wait until she is of age, be refused on religious grounds, and go on writing to her. The sources contradict one another about her birth year, her age at that first meeting, and her age at death.
suggested_refs: Ruskin's drawings and letters concerning Rose La Touche, begun 1858

stops.name: Turin, the Veronese and the sermon
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1858; the day is not recorded and the month is reconstructed from the tour
stops.campa: In the gallery at Turin he sits down before Veronese's Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, a wall of silk and gold and healthy flesh, having spent that morning in a small Waldensian chapel hearing a preacher consign the rest of the human race to perdition. He sets the two against each other, and the Evangelical faith his mother built into him gives way in an afternoon. He calls it his unconversion. He does not become an unbeliever. He stops being able to say that beauty and God stand on opposite sides of a room.
suggested_refs: Veronese's Solomon and the Queen of Sheba, Galleria Sabauda, Turin, and the Waldensian temple in the same city

stops.name: Denmark Hill, Unto This Last
stops.date_confidence: serialisation attested August to November 1860; day not recorded
stops.campa: The fifth and last volume of Modern Painters appears, seventeen years after the first, and in the same season the Cornhill Magazine begins printing four essays in which the most admired art critic in England attacks the whole science of political economy. He denies that a nation's wealth is its money, denies that a labour market is a natural law, and writes that there is no wealth but life. The subscribers revolt and the series is stopped after the fourth. Collected as a book in 1862, it sells for years to almost nobody.
suggested_refs: Unto This Last, serialised in the Cornhill Magazine, August to November 1860, and issued as a volume in 1862

stops.name: Denmark Hill, the death of the father
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: John James Ruskin dies on the third of March. The estate is enormous, reported between one hundred and twenty and one hundred and fifty-seven thousand pounds, with houses, land, and the Turner drawings his son has been cataloguing by hand for years. At forty-five Ruskin is rich on his own account for the first time, and free of the man who read every proof sheet he ever wrote and paid for every book he ever published. He begins giving the money away almost at once, and lives long enough to spend nearly all of it.
suggested_refs: The Turner Bequest drawings at the National Gallery, catalogued by Ruskin over years of unpaid work

stops.name: Winnington Hall, The Ethics of the Dust
stops.date_confidence: the book's publication is attested to 1866; the visits run through the 1859-1868 span and no single date is fixed, so the day and month are defaults
stops.campa: For years he goes down to a girls' school at Winnington in Cheshire, pays its debts, keeps a room of his own in the house, and teaches Bible, geology, mineralogy, and drawing to pupils who treat him as an uncle. The dialogues he holds with them over a tray of crystals become The Ethics of the Dust, a book in which the laws of crystallisation are also the laws of a decent society: the honest atom takes its place in the lattice and does not push its neighbour out. The reviewers find it eccentric. He goes on going down.
suggested_refs: Winnington Hall, Northwich, Cheshire, and the crystal dialogues published as The Ethics of the Dust, 1866

stops.name: Oxford, the first Slade Professor
stops.date_confidence: the appointment is attested to 1869; the Ruskin School of Drawing referred to in the campa was not founded until 1871
stops.campa: Oxford makes him the first Slade Professor of Fine Art, and the lecture rooms will not hold the people who come to hear him. He gives his own money and his own drawings, two years later, to found a school of drawing in the university, so that men may be taught to see before they are taught to compose. The chair is the summit of his public standing and he holds it for ten years. He holds it also through the years in which the mind that fills those rooms begins, out of public sight, to come apart.
stops.quote: life without industry is guilt, and industry without art is brutality: and for the words 'good' and 'wicked,' used of men, you may almost substitute the words 'Makers' and 'Destroyers.'
stops.quote_source: John Ruskin, Lectures on Art (Oxford, Hilary Term 1870), Lecture III, 'The Relation of Art to Morals,' section 95
suggested_refs: The Ruskin School of Drawing, Oxford, founded 1871 with Ruskin's own endowment and teaching collection
sources: John Ruskin, Lectures on Art, Project Gutenberg ebook 19164

stops.name: Denmark Hill, Fors Clavigera and the Guild of St George
stops.date_confidence: Fors Clavigera Letter I is dated 1 January 1871 and the Guild is attested to 1871; the day-precise founding date of the Guild given by some sources is not supported by anything reachable
stops.campa: He begins Fors Clavigera, letters to the workmen and labourers of Great Britain, printed monthly, priced at a figure the trade hates, sold outside the booksellers, and written in whatever voice the month requires: Homer, mineralogy, the price of bread, his own dreams. In the same year he founds the company that becomes the Guild of St George, gives it a tenth of his fortune, and asks England's landowners to match him. Almost none do. The Guild buys land and a museum, and it is still a going concern.
suggested_refs: Fors Clavigera, Letter I, 1 January 1871, and the founding subscription of the Guild of St George

stops.name: Brantwood, the house on the far shore
stops.date_confidence: purchase attested to 1871 and occupation to 1872; the month is reconstructed
stops.campa: He buys a plain house on the far shore of Coniston Water, sight unseen, and finds it half a ruin with the best view in England. He adds a turret to his bedroom so as to see the lake in every direction, plants the moor, cuts a harbour, and puts up a lodge for his valet's family. He is fifty-three, his mother is dead, Denmark Hill is given up, and he has come to live within sight of the fells he first saw from a carriage window as a boy. He will die in this house twenty-eight years from now.
suggested_refs: Brantwood, Coniston, with Ruskin's turret bedroom window over the lake

stops.name: Sheffield, the museum at Walkley
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1875; day and month not recorded, and the April date is a reconstruction
stops.campa: The Guild opens a museum in a cottage at Walkley, high on the hill above the Sheffield steel works, and fills it with minerals, casts of cathedral ornament, illuminated manuscripts, and drawings by Turner. It is put up the hill deliberately: the men of the grinding shops are meant to walk to it after work. He wants them to see in one room the crystal as it grows and the leaf as a mason cut it in the thirteenth century. The collection outlives him and stays in Sheffield, held by the Guild he founded for it.
suggested_refs: St George's Museum, Walkley, Sheffield, and the Ruskin Collection now in the Millennium Galleries
sources: General Ruskin biographical record, St George's Museum

stops.name: Dublin, the death of Rose La Touche
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; the cause of death is disputed among sources and is not adjudicated here
stops.campa: Rose La Touche dies in a Dublin nursing home at twenty-seven, after years of religious mania and refusal of food, having refused him, written to him, and refused him again. The sources disagree about what killed her and even about the year she was born. Ruskin is fifty-six. Her letters, the drawings he made of her, and the private accounting he keeps of the whole seventeen years run under the rest of his life and surface in Fors Clavigera in forms his readers cannot always follow.
suggested_refs: Rose La Touche's grave and the Harristown letters preserved among Ruskin's papers

stops.name: Brantwood, Fors Clavigera Letter 79
stops.date_confidence: the letter is dated 2 July 1877 and is attested; the place of writing is not fixed by the sources and the pin is Brantwood by default
stops.campa: In the July letter he turns on a picture hanging at the new Grosvenor Gallery: Whistler's Nocturne in Black and Gold, a dark canvas with a scatter of falling sparks, priced at two hundred guineas. He writes that Sir Coutts Lindsay should never have admitted a work in which the artist's conceit so nearly approaches wilful imposture, and then adds the sentence that costs him a trial. He is fifty-eight, has been in print for forty years, and has never in his life been sued for anything he wrote.
stops.quote: For Mr. Whistler's own sake, no less than for the protection of the purchaser, Sir Coutts Lindsay ought not to have admitted works into the gallery in which the ill-educated conceit of the artist so nearly approached the aspect of wilful imposture. I have seen, and heard, much of Cockney impudence before now; but never expected to hear a coxcomb ask two hundred guineas for flinging a pot of paint in the public's face.
stops.quote_source: John Ruskin, Fors Clavigera, Letter LXXIX, July 1877, page 73 (archive.org, forsclavigera04ruskiala)
suggested_refs: Whistler, Nocturne in Black and Gold: The Falling Rocket, exhibited at the Grosvenor Gallery, 1877

stops.name: Brantwood, the delirium
stops.date_confidence: attested to February 1878; day not recorded. Sources disagree on how to number it: an earlier collapse at Matlock in 1871 is also on record
stops.campa: In February, at Brantwood, the mind gives way. He believes himself in combat with the devil in his own bedroom; the attack runs for weeks and leaves him unfit to appear in a court that is waiting for him. It is not the first collapse, there had been one at Matlock in Derbyshire in 1871, but it is the first of the violent delirious attacks, and after it the pattern is set for twelve years: work, exaltation, a fortnight of madness, a long silence, and work again. He is fifty-nine years old.
suggested_refs: The 1878 Brantwood attack, described in Ruskin's own later account of his illnesses

stops.name: Westminster, the farthing
stops.date_confidence: attested to 25 November 1878; the pin is the Westminster courts, where the superior common-law courts still sat, and not the Royal Courts of Justice on the Strand, which did not open until 1882
stops.campa: Whistler sues for libel and the case is heard in the Exchequer Division before Baron Huddleston. Ruskin is too ill to attend and is defended by counsel. The jury finds for Whistler and awards him one farthing in damages, the smallest coin in circulation, without costs. The costs fall on Whistler, who is bankrupt within the year. The verdict leaves standing the rule that a critic may be answerable at law for what he writes about a picture. Ruskin gives up the Oxford chair the following year and says the trial is the reason.
suggested_refs: The Whistler v. Ruskin trial record, Exchequer Division, 25-26 November 1878, and the farthing Whistler afterwards wore on his watch chain
sources: Wikipedia, 'Nocturne in Black and Gold: The Falling Rocket'

stops.name: Oxford, the chair given up
stops.date_confidence: the 1879 resignation is attested; the month is reconstructed. The two resignations are frequently transposed in secondary accounts: 1879 was health and the Whistler trial, 1884 was vivisection
stops.campa: He gives up the Slade chair, worn down by illness and finally by the trial, and Oxford loses the man who filled its lecture rooms. He comes back to it in 1883 for two years of lectures so wild and so brilliant that his friends beg him to stop, and resigns a second time in 1884 when the university votes money for a physiological laboratory: he will not hold a chair in a place that practises vivisection. He holds no post after that. Fors Clavigera runs on to 1884, and the Guild's business reaches him at Brantwood by post.
suggested_refs: Ruskin's two tenures of the Slade Professorship, 1869-1879 and 1883-1884

stops.name: Amiens, the Bible in stone
stops.date_confidence: the Bible of Amiens work runs 1880-1885; the month and day here are defaults on the opening year
stops.campa: He goes back to the west front of Amiens and reads it: the prophets along the porches, the virtues and the vices in their quatrefoils, the Christ of the central door, carved stone treated as a book written for people who could not read one. The Bible of Amiens comes out of it, part of a project for the young that he never finishes. Twenty-four years later Marcel Proust, whose English is poor, translates it into French with his mother's help and Marie Nordlinger's, and says he does not claim to know English, he claims to know Ruskin.
suggested_refs: The west front of Amiens Cathedral and Proust's 1904 La Bible d'Amiens with its long preface
sources: General Ruskin biographical record, The Bible of Amiens

stops.name: Brantwood, Praeterita
stops.date_confidence: serialisation begins 1885 and breaks off unfinished in 1889; month and day are defaults
stops.campa: In the intervals between attacks he begins an autobiography written in scenes: the walled garden at Herne Hill, the falls at Schaffhausen, the aspen at Fontainebleau, a picture in a gallery at Turin. He calls it Praeterita, things past, and leaves the marriage out of it altogether. The prose is the clearest he ever wrote and he writes it while losing the power to write anything. It breaks off in 1889 in the middle of a chapter, and after that sentence he publishes nothing for the eleven years he has left.
suggested_refs: Praeterita, issued in parts from 1885 and left unfinished in 1889

stops.name: Brantwood, the last silence
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; some accounts pin the death at Coniston village, but the house is Brantwood
stops.campa: He dies at Brantwood on the twentieth of January, in the first month of the new century, aged eighty. The last eleven years have been almost wordless: he sits at the window above Coniston Water, the household kept quiet around him, most visitors turned away at the door. He has published nothing since Praeterita broke off. Four months from now a young Frenchman takes a room at the Danieli to translate him, and four years from now a lawyer in Natal reads Unto This Last on a night train.
suggested_refs: Brantwood, the turret bedroom, and Ruskin's last years in silence

stops.name: Coniston, the churchyard at St Andrew's
stops.date_confidence: burial five days after the death is attested; the description of the memorial cross is a reconstruction, and the sources disagree over whether Ruskin or his executors declined Westminster Abbey
stops.campa: Westminster Abbey is offered and declined, and he is buried five days after his death in the churchyard at Coniston according to his own wish, under a shaft of green Tilberthwaite slate carved with knotwork and with panels alluding to his books. It stands across the water from the house he watched the lake from for twenty-eight years. Within a year the village opens a museum to him. His own collection stays in Sheffield, in the town and among the working men it was bought for.
suggested_refs: The Ruskin cross in St Andrew's churchyard, Coniston, in green Tilberthwaite slate

stops.name: Venice, the Danieli again
stops.date_confidence: attested to May 1900 from marcel_proust.journey.json; day not recorded. Pin inherited byte-identical from that file
stops.campa: Four months after the funeral a French asthmatic of twenty-eight takes a room at the Danieli, the hotel where Ruskin lodged with his wife in 1849, and reads The Stones of Venice on the marble floor of Saint Mark's with the book open on his knees. Marcel Proust is learning from a dead Englishman how to build a cathedral out of prose. In 1876 William Morris had brought his wife Jane to this same city, out of whose stones Ruskin made the book that converted him; no record survives of what she thought of it.
stops.quote: I do not claim to know English, I claim to know Ruskin.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Marcel Proust, cited in marcel_proust.journey.json
suggested_refs: Proust's 1900 Venice notebooks and the marble pavement of the Basilica di San Marco

stops.name: Durban, the night train
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1904 from mahatma_gandhi.journey.json; day not recorded, defaulted to 01
stops.campa: On a station platform Henry Polak hands a lawyer of thirty-four a book to read on the overnight train to Durban. Mohandas Gandhi opens Unto This Last between dark and morning and does not sleep. Within weeks he has bought land at Phoenix in Natal and founded a settlement on its principles: that the good of the one is contained in the good of all, that a lawyer's work is worth no more than a barber's, that a life of labour on the land is the only life worth having. The book had ruined its author's reputation in 1860.
suggested_refs: Gandhi's Gujarati paraphrase of Unto This Last, published as Sarvodaya, and the Phoenix Settlement in Natal
